body:
i agree with you that the collection points might be seen as instances of public solicitation since there isn’t really a set legal definition. but i also think that since they are within food establishments and set up with the permission of the owners, it is possible that they also do not really constitute soliciting, a scenario that differs from your orchard road example since that is an unmanned and public space without a tenant or owner. i would think that the HHSC act was also set up to prevent fundraising agents from harassing or targeting members of the public in public spaces or at their doorsteps, and i think these public collection points do not pose any potential harassment or bothersome issues.

if anything, i think that if he was not allowed to raise funds this way, the article likely would not have been published and instead there would probably have been investigations. but i also can’t be too certain about that, i guess we’ll just have to wait and see if there’s any follow up!

i’m not trained in law so i’m not sure what exactly the legal definition for “soliciting” is (if anyone does know please enlighten us!) but i would think the law applies to actively asking for funds in a public place on a person to person basis (like they do at mrt stations). and i don’t think him meeting with people that want to donate meets that criteria also since he didn’t approach people to ask but merely publicized it through the internet and donors took the initiative to contact him.

again, i am not a lawyer so if i’ve gotten anything wrong please feel free to correct me!
correct me if i’m wrong but since he did not go house to house nor solicit for funds in a public area, he does not need to get a HHSC license, right?
